paragraphs: Passive learning receives labeled examples without choosing which labels to request. Active learning instead selects examples for labeling, aiming to reach a desired accuracy with fewer labels. This paper asks whether an existing passive learning algorithm can be transformed into an active one that has a provable advantage even when some training labels are incorrect.

The authors prove that such a transformation is possible for any VC class, a family of classifiers whose complexity is described through its ability to fit label patterns. The improvement applies to every nontrivial distribution satisfying a uniform classification noise condition. Its scope is therefore broad across classifier families but explicitly restricted in the kind of label noise it permits.

The guarantee concerns strong asymptotic improvements in label complexity: how labeling requirements compare as learning becomes increasingly demanding. It extends a corresponding result for the realizable setting to a noisy setting. The significance is that restricted classification noise still permits a general theoretical advantage from choosing which examples to label.
icml-2013-activized-learning-with-unifor.tldr: A general transformation gives passive learners asymptotically better label efficiency through active learning under uniform classification noise.

paragraphs: Regression usually seeks a predictive relationship in observed data. This paper studies a setting where an adversary can influence how those data are generated. The learner and adversary have conflicting goals, but their interests need not be exact opposites. That distinction allows the problem to represent strategic interference without requiring a completely antagonistic relationship.

The learner also lacks complete information about the adversary's objective. The proposed framework expresses available knowledge about parameters of that objective through a Bayesian prior. It then treats prediction and interference as a Bayesian game, so the learner's strategy accounts for uncertainty about what the adversary is trying to accomplish.

The theoretical contribution identifies conditions under which this game has a unique Bayesian equilibrium. This is a conditional result about a well-defined strategic solution. Experiments compare the resulting strategy with Nash equilibrium, minimax, and ordinary linear regression strategies. These comparisons examine different ways of handling strategic uncertainty; the abstract does not state that any one strategy wins universally.
icml-2013-bayesian-games-for-adversarial.tldr: The paper models adversarial regression as a Bayesian game that accounts for uncertainty about the adversary's goals.

paragraphs: Kernel methods can learn through similarity evaluations without directly accessing training features. This paper asks how to provide differential privacy under that restriction. Releasing a private predictor for general kernels in the unrestricted setting is impossible, so the authors develop three practical settings that change what information is available or what must be released.

In the first, a trusted learner receives test points and returns private predictions. In the second, the learner releases a private parameter vector after seeing a small subset of unlabeled test data. In the third, the learner need not see test data, but the kernel must be efficiently computable over a low-dimensional vector space.

Each setting receives a learning algorithm with a provable utility or error bound. The methods also apply to a previously studied setting, where their sample-complexity bounds depend on dimension through O(d^(1/3)), compared with O(d^(1/2)) for existing methods at the same generalization error. The contribution shows how specific changes to the learning arrangement can make private kernel learning possible and improve its dimensional dependence.
icml-2013-differentially-private-learnin.tldr: Three practical restrictions enable private kernel learning with error guarantees and improved dimensional dependence in an established setting.

paragraphs: Visual recognition benefits from representations that remain useful when an object's appearance changes across views. Feature pooling networks are widely used to build such representations. This paper explores directly modeling complex invariances in object features as a way to improve recognition, alongside approaches that learn additional invariances or process larger amounts of training data.

The authors introduce a dictionary learning algorithm that incorporates these complex invariances. Dictionary learning constructs a collection of feature components used to represent inputs. Here, directly accounting for invariance becomes part of that construction. The algorithm is described as simple, applicable to most feature pooling network settings, and requiring no additional tuning.

Experiments report competitive and state-of-the-art recognition accuracy on datasets including CIFAR-10 and STL-10. These findings support direct invariance modeling as a useful approach in the tested settings. The paper also discusses what the results imply about the usefulness of pretrained features and how explicit modeling can contribute to broader efforts to learn invariant representations.
icml-2013-direct-modeling-of-complex-inv.tldr: Directly modeling complex feature invariances yields a simple dictionary learning method with competitive visual recognition results.

paragraphs: Ranking objects from pairwise comparisons means turning observations about individual pairs into an overall ordering. The paper considers situations where comparisons arrive passively and noisily, rather than being chosen by the learner. This matters because only a subset of the possible pairs may be observed, while centralized optimization methods can be awkward to adapt to online or distributed operation.

The authors show that much simpler algorithms can match the linear sample-complexity lower bound in expectation for a fixed expected Kendall tau error. This error measures disagreement between rankings through their pairwise orderings. The result connects algorithmic simplicity with a strong statistical guarantee, showing that the targeted accuracy need not require a centralized optimization procedure.

With an average of O(n log n) binary comparisons, the algorithms offer different guarantees: one recovers the true ranking in a uniform sense, while another predicts the top more accurately than the bottom. The paper also discusses online and distributed extensions, connecting these statistical results to settings where comparisons and computation are spread over time or across participants.
icml-2013-efficient-ranking-from-pairwis.tldr: Simple ranking algorithms achieve strong sample-efficiency guarantees from passive, noisy comparisons and support online or distributed extensions.

paragraphs: A stochastic bandit learner repeatedly chooses among actions with uncertain rewards, balancing exploration with use of the best options found so far. This paper adapts that problem to a peer-to-peer network. Every peer has the same available actions and can independently choose one action during each iteration.

After acting, peers communicate with a few randomly selected peers. This limited, gossip-style communication provides a way to share information gathered across the network. The central question is whether decentralized learners can turn their collective observations into faster learning despite communicating with only a small part of the network at each step.

The authors prove a linear speedup with the number of participating peers. More precisely, after an iteration threshold on the order of log N, the probability that a peer selects a suboptimal action is proportional to 1/(Nt), where N is the number of peers and t is the iteration. Simulations support the theoretical result and show graceful scaling with network size in the evaluated settings.
icml-2013-gossip-based-distributed-stoch.tldr: Limited random communication lets peer-to-peer bandit learners achieve a provable linear learning speedup with network size.

paragraphs: A signal need not be sparse in its original coordinates to have useful sparse structure. This paper studies recovery when applying a linear transformation D produces a sparse vector. The estimator combines a squared measurement-error term with an absolute-value penalty on the transformed signal, encouraging sparsity in Dθ while fitting the observations.

The analysis assumes a Gaussian random measurement matrix and, for noisy observations, independent centered sub-Gaussian noise. With a bounded condition number for D, the authors establish high-probability exact recovery in the noiseless case using measurements on the order of s log p. In the noisy case, estimation error converges to zero almost surely when s log p grows more slowly than the measurement count.

The results agree with the LASSO special case where D is the identity and improve existing analysis. The condition number of D is central: the paper examines bounds for fused LASSO and random-graph transformations, including a graph-density condition for the latter. Numerical simulations are consistent with the theoretical findings.
icml-2013-guaranteed-sparse-recovery-und.tldr: The paper proves conditional recovery guarantees for signals that become sparse under a linear transformation.

paragraphs: Direct policy search adjusts a controller to improve its behavior, but searching over policies with hundreds of parameters can require many samples and lead to poor local solutions. This paper introduces guided policy search, which uses trajectory optimization to provide direction for learning a policy in a high-dimensional control problem.

The approach uses differential dynamic programming to generate guiding samples. These samples represent trajectories that can inform the controller's search. A regularized, importance-sampled policy optimization procedure then incorporates them into policy learning. The key connection is between optimizing trajectories and using the resulting experience to shape a more general controller.

The method is evaluated by learning neural network controllers for planar swimming, hopping, and walking, together with simulated three-dimensional humanoid running. These tasks place the proposed guidance mechanism in varied movement settings. The contribution is a concrete way to steer complex policy learning toward useful behavior and away from poor local optima, addressing difficulties that arise when policy search must discover effective behavior through sampling.
icml-2013-guided-policy-search-57b60ad93.tldr: Guided policy search uses optimized trajectories to steer the learning of complex neural network controllers.

paragraphs: Related classification tasks can benefit from learning together, but choosing how much they should share is difficult. This paper develops a hierarchical method for sharing information across tasks in both multitask and multiclass settings. It addresses the problem without requiring fixed decisions about which tasks belong in the same group.

The method follows a top-down sequence of optimization problems. It begins with a strong incentive for broad sharing across all classes, then gradually reduces that incentive until tasks are treated separately. This cascade lets learning exploit several levels of sharing within a collection of related tasks, moving from common structure toward task-specific distinctions.

To handle problems with many tasks and classes, the authors extend the batch method to an online setting and provide regret analysis. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets report significant improvements over baseline and state-of-the-art methods. Together, the algorithm and analysis support a gradual approach to information sharing, while the experiments demonstrate its advantages in the evaluated classification problems.
icml-2013-hierarchical-regularization-ca.tldr: A hierarchy of progressively weaker sharing incentives improves joint classifier learning without imposing fixed task groups.

paragraphs: Single-molecule experiments observe biological processes indirectly through noisy signals, such as fluorescence intensity or bead position. Several recordings may describe the same underlying process while differing because of measurement artifacts and variability between signals. These differences make it difficult to combine recordings into one account of the process.

Hidden Markov models describe such data using unobserved conformational states, transitions between states, and transition rates. Straightforward analyses of separate recordings require ad hoc post-processing to combine their conclusions. The paper instead develops a hierarchically coupled HMM that connects individual time series within a shared model, allowing inter-signal variability to be handled automatically and systematically.

The learning procedure combines generalized expectation maximization for point estimates of shared hyperparameters with variational Bayesian inference for individual time series. This division connects the treatment of each recording to the estimation of an overall model. The intended result is a single interpretable representation of the data-generating process, supporting the study of molecular states and kinetic rates across heterogeneous measurements.
icml-2013-hierarchically-coupled-hidden-.tldr: A hierarchical HMM combines heterogeneous single-molecule recordings into one interpretable model of states and transition rates.

paragraphs: Pattern-based conditional random fields assign scores to label sequences using predefined patterns. A term contributes when the labels across a particular interval exactly match its specified pattern. This gives sequence tagging models a way to express relationships involving whole label substrings, while creating computational challenges for inference.

The paper develops faster algorithms for three central tasks: computing the partition function that normalizes probabilities, computing marginal probabilities, and finding the highest-probability labeling. Their respective complexities are O(nL), O(nLℓmax), and O(nL min{|D|, log(ℓmax + 1)}). Here n is sequence length, L is total pattern length, ℓmax is the longest pattern, and D is the alphabet.

These bounds improve on the previous algorithms described in the abstract, reducing dependence on alphabet size and other pattern-related quantities. The authors also provide an efficient sampling algorithm and revisit highest-probability inference with non-positive weights. An application to protein dihedral-angle prediction connects the computational advances to a concrete sequence prediction problem.
icml-2013-inference-algorithms-for-patte.tldr: The paper accelerates normalization, marginal computation, and optimal labeling for sequence CRFs built from predefined patterns.

paragraphs: When an object moves, an image changes both because of what is depicted and because of the transformation between views. This paper studies how to learn representations that separate those two sources of variation. It starts from the energy model, a biologically inspired method for extracting relationships between images in motion analysis and stereopsis.

The proposed modification adds another pooling layer. The authors show that this makes it possible to learn two complementary encodings: representations of transformations that are mostly insensitive to image content, and representations of images that are mostly insensitive to observed transformations. The qualification matters because the claimed invariance is substantial rather than complete.

The paper connects this mechanism to learning object features that are invariant to three-dimensional pose by watching videos of objects. It evaluates the approach on videos derived from the NORB dataset. The contribution is a route from observed image relationships to useful invariance, with the extra pooling layer supporting the separation of object appearance from changes in viewpoint.
icml-2013-learning-invariant-features-by.tldr: An extra pooling layer helps an energy model learn largely separate representations of image content and transformations from video.

paragraphs: Demonstrations can contain several behaviors without labels identifying which behavior each recording represents. Their measured trajectories may overlap heavily even when the underlying controllers are easier to distinguish. This paper learns multiple motor primitives by seeking a latent controller representation in which those behaviors can be separated.

The method uses a Dirichlet process mixture model to cluster observed time series while recovering sparse representations of the behaviors. A Laplacian prior serves as the process's base measure and supplies the sparse modeling component. Clustering and representation learning therefore happen together, allowing the inferred controller structure to help organize demonstrations that are mixed in measurement space.

For linear models, including potential functions built as linear combinations of many features, the authors show that the observation marginal can be calculated analytically. This enables an efficient sampler for learning the model. Evaluations use robot behaviors and real human-motion data and compare the method with other techniques, examining its ability to discover multiple behaviors from unlabeled observations.
icml-2013-learning-multiple-behaviors-fr.tldr: A Dirichlet process mixture jointly clusters unlabeled motion demonstrations and learns sparse latent controller representations.

paragraphs: Change-point detection divides a signal into segments by locating positions where its behavior changes. Segmentation models commonly choose the number of changes through a cost function that penalizes additional change-points. The penalty therefore affects the segmentation directly: it controls how readily the model introduces another boundary in the signal.

This paper proposes learning the penalty and its constants from a database of signals with weak change-point annotations. The approach uses available annotations to guide a choice that otherwise must be supplied to the segmentation model. It formulates the learning task as an interval regression problem and introduces a convex relaxation, making the resulting optimization amenable to accelerated proximal gradient methods.

The method achieves state-of-the-art change-point detection on an annotated database of DNA copy-number profiles from neuroblastoma tumors. This finding supports learning segmentation penalties from weak supervision in that application. The broader methodological contribution is to make penalty selection itself a learnable component, connecting annotated examples to the rule used to choose how many changes a signal contains.
icml-2013-learning-sparse-penalties-for-.tldr: Learning segmentation penalties from weak annotations improves change-point detection on a database of tumor DNA copy-number profiles.

paragraphs: Network estimation often seeks relationships among nodes described by one variable each. Many applications instead attach entire feature vectors to nodes, including image, text, or multiple-view attributes. This paper addresses the resulting mismatch between multi-attribute data and graph estimation methods developed around scalar variables and Gaussian covariance selection.

The proposed framework estimates partial canonical correlations instead of partial correlations. This change accommodates relationships between groups of features associated with different nodes. It makes the multivariate structure of each node part of the estimation problem, providing a principled way to infer a graph when a node cannot be adequately represented by a single attribute.

The authors develop an efficient algorithm that uses the multi-attribute structure and establish sufficient conditions for consistent graph recovery. These conditions provide a theoretical route to recovering the underlying graph; they are not stated as necessary conditions for success. Extensive simulations examine the method under varied conditions, complementing the recovery theory with empirical evidence about its performance.
icml-2013-markov-network-estimation-from.tldr: Partial canonical correlations enable principled graph estimation when each node carries multiple attributes.

paragraphs: Multiple instance learning represents an example as a collection of instances, helping capture local objects or components. Traditional learning often represents the same example with one global feature vector. MILEAGE brings these representations together so that a classifier can use both local information and a description of the example as a whole.

Within this framework, the authors formulate a large-margin method that learns the classifier while adjusting the weights assigned to global and multiple-instance features. These weights adapt for each example. The approach therefore allows different examples to rely on the two representations to different degrees, instead of imposing one common balance across the dataset.

The resulting optimization problem is nonconvex. The proposed solution extends the bundle method to this setting, and the paper analyzes properties including convergence rate and generalization error rate. Experiments demonstrate advantages over several state-of-the-art multiple instance and traditional learning methods. The findings support jointly learning how to combine the representations and how to classify with them.
icml-2013-mileage-multiple-instance-lear.tldr: MILEAGE learns an example-specific balance between global features and multiple-instance representations while training a classifier.

paragraphs: Multiple kernel learning uses several notions of similarity when constructing a classifier. For multiclass problems, the challenge is to choose kernels in a way that supports separation among several possible labels. This paper introduces a multiclass margin associated with a kernel and makes that quantity the basis of a new learning approach.

The authors show that larger values of this margin guarantee the existence of an accurate multiclass predictor. They then define M^3K, a family of algorithms that maximize the kernel's multiclass margin. The objective therefore has a theoretical connection to prediction quality, giving the learning procedure a direct criterion for evaluating the usefulness of a kernel.

The theoretical analysis includes new multiclass Rademacher complexity margin bounds, which relate the richness of the predictor family and its margins to generalization. Experiments on several datasets include comparisons where the method improves on state-of-the-art algorithms for both binary and multiclass multiple-kernel classification. Those results complement the theoretical justification with evidence of practical benefits in the tested comparisons.
icml-2013-multi-class-classification-wit.tldr: M^3K learns with multiple kernels by maximizing a multiclass margin linked theoretically to accurate prediction.

paragraphs: One-bit compressed sensing keeps only the signs of linear measurements of a sparse signal. The paper studies how to design both the measurement matrix and an efficient recovery algorithm under this severe reduction in information. It separates two objectives: identifying which coordinates are nonzero and approximating the direction of the signal.

For support recovery, the authors propose two constructions based on union-free families of sets and expanders. Their methods are universal in the stated sense that one measurement matrix can recover almost all signals. This shared-matrix property matters because the measurement design can serve a broad collection of sparse signals rather than being tailored to each individual input.

For approximate vector recovery, the target is a unit vector close to the original signal after normalization. The paper proposes a method using a near-optimal number of measurements. Experiments also show recovery with fewer measurements than several existing methods in the evaluated settings. Together, the results address both locating sparse structure and reconstructing signal direction from sign-only observations.
icml-2013-one-bit-compressed-sensing-pro.tldr: Combinatorial measurement designs and recovery algorithms identify sparse supports and approximate signal directions from sign-only measurements.

paragraphs: Crowdsourced labels cost money, and a fixed budget must be divided among tasks and workers. Tasks differ in ambiguity, while workers differ in expertise, so choosing which instance-worker pair to fund affects overall label quality. This paper treats that allocation as a sequential decision problem in which each purchased label informs later choices.

The authors begin with a setting that assumes perfect workers and formulate allocation as a Bayesian Markov decision process. Dynamic programming can produce an optimal policy for a specified budget, but it is computationally intractable. The proposed optimistic knowledge gradient policy supplies a practically efficient approximation with a theoretical consistency guarantee.

The framework is then extended to heterogeneous workers and tasks with contextual information. These extensions bring worker differences and task descriptions into the allocation problem. Experiments on simulated and real data report superior performance for the proposed method. The contribution combines a formal account of optimal budget allocation with an approximation that makes sequential allocation practical.
icml-2013-optimistic-knowledge-gradient-.tldr: An optimistic knowledge gradient policy efficiently approximates Bayesian budget allocation for crowdsourced labeling.

paragraphs: Learning related tasks together can provide more information than training each task independently. This paper studies sparse coding and dictionary learning as a way to organize that shared information in multitask and transfer learning. Its central assumption is that task parameters can be approximated well using sparse linear combinations of common dictionary atoms.

Each task therefore draws on only a small selection of components from a shared dictionary, even when the parameter space is high-dimensional or infinite-dimensional. The assumption, together with the quantity of data available across tasks, supports a principled choice of dictionary. Sharing occurs through reusable components while allowing tasks to use different combinations.

The authors derive generalization error bounds for both multitask and transfer learning. Experiments on one synthetic and two real datasets show advantages over independent task learning, an approach based on orthogonal dense task representations, and a related task-grouping method. These findings support sparse shared representations in the evaluated settings, while the theory explains the approach under its stated approximation assumption.
icml-2013-sparse-coding-for-multitask-an.tldr: A shared dictionary of sparsely combined components supports multitask and transfer learning with generalization bounds and empirical gains.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised classification uses labeled and unlabeled examples together. This paper proposes squared-loss mutual information regularization, or SMIR, for classifiers that assign probabilities across multiple classes. It follows the information maximization principle, using an information-based criterion to guide learning beyond the information supplied by labeled examples alone.

A central feature is that SMIR is convex under mild conditions. This addresses the nonconvexity associated with mutual information regularization and gives the proposed formulation a useful optimization property. The method also provides an analytical solution, predictions for previously unseen inputs, multiclass classification, and probabilistic outputs. These capabilities connect its mathematical formulation to common requirements of a usable classifier.

The paper derives new generalization error bounds and reports experiments in which SMIR compares favorably with state-of-the-art methods. The bounds supply theoretical support, while the experiments establish favorable behavior in the evaluated settings. Its contribution is an information-theoretic regularizer that combines conditional convexity with several practical classification capabilities in one semi-supervised approach.
icml-2013-squared-loss-mutual-informatio.tldr: SMIR offers information-based semi-supervised classification with conditional convexity, an analytical solution, and multiclass probabilistic predictions.

paragraphs: A discrete integral adds contributions across a set of possibilities. When that set grows exponentially with the number of variables, direct summation quickly becomes impractical. This paper proposes a randomized method that approximates a general discrete integral within a constant factor with high probability, addressing the cost of reasoning over such enormous spaces.

The algorithm uses a small number of discrete combinatorial optimization problems with randomly generated parity constraints. These constraints act as a hash function, organizing the original space through randomized restrictions. The approach turns an integration task into a limited collection of constrained optimization tasks, connecting the ability to find good configurations with the ability to estimate an aggregate over configurations.

As an application, the authors approximate the partition function of a discrete graphical model using a small number of maximum a posteriori queries. The partition function normalizes the model's probabilities and can support marginal computation or model selection. The stated guarantee is a high-probability constant-factor approximation, giving a precise form of approximate integration rather than an exact sum.
icml-2013-taming-the-curse-of-dimensiona.tldr: Random parity constraints turn a small number of optimization queries into a high-probability constant-factor approximation of discrete integrals.

paragraphs: Factor analysis explains variation through hidden variables whose effects combine additively. This paper addresses data generated by several groups of hidden factors that interact multiplicatively. It introduces Tensor Analyzers, a multilinear extension of Factor Analyzers designed to represent these interactions within the model of how observations are produced.

Learning requires inference about the hidden factor values. The authors describe an efficient way to sample from their posterior distribution and show how those samples can be used inside expectation maximization. They demonstrate this procedure by learning mixture models of natural image patches, connecting the richer latent structure to a concrete image-modeling task.

Tensor Analyzers also recognize faces accurately under substantial pose and illumination changes when only one previous image of a face is available. The paper further shows that training can be unsupervised, semi-supervised, or fully supervised. These findings illustrate both the representational value of multiplicative factors and the model's ability to accommodate different amounts of labeling information.
icml-2013-tensor-analyzers-405c6ac12d.tldr: Tensor Analyzers extend factor analysis to interacting latent factors, supporting image modeling and face recognition across pose and lighting changes.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning theory often relies on structural assumptions about the environment to bound how much experience learning requires. This paper studies sample complexity without assuming that environments are finite or ergodic. It asks what other property of an environment class can make finite learning bounds possible in such a general setting.

The authors define a topology on the space of environments and prove that compactness under this topology is sufficient for finite sample-complexity bounds. They also provide an algorithm that achieves those bounds. Compactness thus supplies a mathematical condition under which a broad environment class remains amenable to learning with a finite bound on required experience.

The paper additionally constructs noncompact environment classes for which finite sample-complexity bounds cannot be achieved. This establishes that some classes outside the compact setting are problematic, without asserting that every noncompact class is unlearnable. A lower bound matches the upper bound apart from logarithmic factors, showing that the achieved dependence is close to the theoretical limit.
icml-2013-the-sample-complexity-of-gener.tldr: Compactness of an environment class yields finite reinforcement learning sample-complexity bounds without finiteness or ergodicity assumptions.

paragraphs: Thompson sampling chooses actions through randomized reasoning about uncertain rewards. This paper develops and analyzes a version for stochastic contextual bandits with linear payoffs, where the information describing available actions can be supplied by an adaptive adversary. The objective is to control regret, the accumulated reward lost relative to better choices.

The algorithm uses a Gaussian prior and Gaussian likelihood. For any algorithm parameter ε between zero and one, the authors prove a high-probability regret bound of order d T^((1+ε)/2) / sqrt(ε), with logarithmic factors suppressed. The result makes explicit how the guarantee depends on context dimension, elapsed time, and the chosen parameter.

The paper presents the first theoretical guarantees for contextual Thompson sampling and describes them as close to the problem's lower bound. Its analysis addresses a previously open question about linear contextual payoffs. The proof uses martingale techniques that also allow extensions to other distributions satisfying specified general conditions, broadening the potential reach of the analytical method beyond the Gaussian construction.
icml-2013-thompson-sampling-for-contextu.tldr: A Gaussian Thompson sampling algorithm receives high-probability regret guarantees for linear contextual bandits with adaptively chosen contexts.
